blocks.text: Theme 2.1 · Accessibility, connectivity and infrastructure · Focus area 8
Cruise added about R1.79bn to provincial GDP-R in 2024/25, and Cape Town's berth took 83 calls against room for 150 or more, so growth comes from ships, excursions and day stops, not port capital.

Cruise has room to grow at the berth Cape Town already has. The equipped berth handled 83 calls in 2024/25 against a season capacity of 150 or more (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p110). That season brought about R1.99bn of spending before displacement and added about R1.79bn to provincial GDP-R after it (StratEcon, Cruise Liner Economic Contribution Study 2024/25, Oct 2025, p4, p19, p20, p22; the study counts 79 vessel visits for the season). Growth here needs product and marketing, not capital works (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p112).

International passengers drive the value (section 2.3). World cruises made up 42 of the 79 vessel visits, and their passengers added R802m to provincial GDP-R, 73% of what all passengers added (StratEcon, Cruise Liner Economic Contribution Study 2024/25, Oct 2025, p4, p23). The season also earned R1.326bn of net foreign exchange and R259m in taxes (StratEcon, Cruise Liner Economic Contribution Study 2024/25, Oct 2025, p28, p34).

Cruise also carries spend beyond the city. Cape Town anchors the itinerary, and Mossel Bay and Saldanha Bay can extend it east and west (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p111). Stakeholders name home porting and expedition vessels as the segments that bring longer stays and higher local spend (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p9).

What limits growth is ships and product, not berths (section 2.3). The equipped berth takes ships of up to 300m, the South-Easter delays berthing and there is no shore power (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p110). Port capital goes to freight: Saldanha's R4bn iron-ore expansion and Cape Town's container expansion add no cruise capacity (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p112).

blocks.message: Cape Town's berth has room and value grows with international passengers; ship size and wind are the constraints, and port capital is going to freight.

blocks.text: The evidence sets a clear stance: protect Cape Town, back Mossel Bay now and watch Saldanha Bay (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p112). Mossel Bay handled 21 calls in 2024/25, opened a new passenger facility in November 2025 and expects about 23 calls next season (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p111). Yet ships anchor and tender there, and only small and mid-sized ships call (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p111). Saldanha Bay has no passenger facility. The regional ports work as day stops rather than home ports, so they spread spend rather than multiply the passenger total (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p111, p112).

Wesgro's plan sets the target: 250 ship calls over FY26 to FY30, about 50 a year. [Summary of Findings, 14 Oct 2026: Cruise Cape Town to confirm that the deck's 250 calls are the plan's five-year total.] The 50 rounds up a 47-call average, the 67 calls of 2023/24 less the 20 calls rerouted to the Cape by the Middle East conflict (Wesgro, Strategic Plan 2025/26 to 2029/30, p20). That pace sits inside the berth's season capacity of 150 or more, so it needs no second berth (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p110).

The approach works with the berth Cape Town has rather than waiting for a new one. Cruise Cape Town leads, and the sequence follows readiness. Line targeting, the Mossel Bay excursion packages and one definition of a call for reporting against the 250 are designed in 2027. Targeting starts with world-cruise lines whose ships fit the 300m berth. Marketing to expedition and home-porting operators follows in 2028, alongside community product on cruise-operator channels (section 4.3). Saldanha Bay waits until demand is proven, because its port capital serves iron ore.

The port itself stays with its owners. Transnet National Ports Authority and the V&A Waterfront hold berth scheduling, wind delays, shore power and the 300m limit. The national ask is that Transnet puts cruise into port planning, since current Western Cape port capital carries none.

blocks.text: The actions match the constraint. The berth has headroom; the gaps are ship-size flexibility, weather reliability and tourism product (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p112). Each line won with ships that fit adds calls without capital works. Packaged excursions give passengers more to buy ashore, and regional day stops spread that spend along the coast (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p112).

The best precedent is local. On its own count, Mossel Bay's calls rose from four before COVID to 27 a season, supported by closer coordination and better excursion packaging (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p20; the Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p111, prints 21 calls for 2024/25). The town credits its partnership with Wesgro (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p21). No benchmark destination offers a cruise precedent, so the case rests on Mossel Bay. The condition is that today's ship deployments hold. Recent growth leans on Red Sea reroutes, and their reversal is the main risk (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p110, p112).
